title: Senior's toolkit: reading certificates and keys
summary: The openssl commands that tell you what a certificate, key or PFX file really holds.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: reading certificates and keys
steps.body: Someone hands you a file called `cert.crt`. Before you install it anywhere, find out what is inside: whose name, which issuer, which dates, which key.

toolkit.what: Prints the whole certificate in readable form: subject, issuer, validity, key type, extensions.
flags: do not print the encoded certificate again
the input is binary DER, not PEM
toolkit.when: the first look at any certificate file

toolkit.what: Just the three facts you usually need, one per line. Easy to paste into a ticket.
Shows the names the certificate is valid for. Clients check the SAN list, not the CN.
flags: what the key may be used for

toolkit.what: A short, unique id for one certificate. Compare it to prove two files are the same certificate.
flags: use SHA-256 (the default SHA-1 is only for old tools)

toolkit.what: Prints the public half of a private key. Hash it next to the certificate's public key to prove they belong together.
flags: show key type and size instead
toolkit.example: openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout | openssl sha256; openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
toolkit.when: "key values mismatch" when a server starts

toolkit.what: Converts a binary DER certificate (often `.cer` from Windows) to PEM text that Linux tools expect.
Checks a PFX/P12 file: asks for the password and lists what it holds, without dumping keys.
flags: OpenSSL 3: open old files encrypted with RC2 (the error mentions `RC2-40-CBC` ... `unsupported`)

toolkit.what: Makes a new private key. P-256 is small, fast and accepted everywhere.
flags: elliptic curve (use `RSA` with `-pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072` if a system needs RSA)
write the key to a file

steps.prompt: Match each option of `openssl x509` to what it prints.
pairs: the DNS names and IPs the certificate covers
a hash that identifies this exact certificate
the name of the CA that signed it

steps.prompt: Print a certificate's subject and validity dates without printing the encoded certificate.
steps.explain: `x509` handles certificates (`req` is for CSRs). `-noout` drops the PEM block, `-dates` prints `notBefore` and `notAfter`.

steps.prompt: nginx refuses to start: `SSL_CTX_use_PrivateKey ... key values mismatch`. You have `cert.pem` and `key.pem`. What do you check first?
options: Hash `openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout` and `openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -pubkey` and compare
steps.explain: The error means the key is not the one the certificate was issued for. If the two public-key hashes differ, find the right key (often the one made with the CSR). Dates and formats are a different error.

steps.prompt: `openssl x509 -in root.cer -noout -text` fails with `Unable to load certificate`. The file came from a Windows admin. Most likely cause?
options: It is binary DER; add `-inform der`
steps.explain: Windows often exports `.cer` as DER. PEM starts with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`; DER is binary. `head -c 30 root.cer` tells you which one you have.

steps.prompt: Which file is safe to email to a colleague, and which must stay secret?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Never install, upload or trust a certificate you have not read: run `-noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName` first and paste it into the ticket. When a server will not start with a new pair, compare the public-key hashes before anything else.
